cards.text: Habakkuk the prophet asked the LORD how long the violence would go on, and the LORD said He's raising up the Chaldeans, a ruthless nation (Habakkuk 1:2, 6). Now Habakkuk answers back, and he starts with who God is: from everlasting, his God, his Holy One. Friend, that's how you open a hard conversation. Start with who you're talking to.

cards.question: Habakkuk tells the LORD He has appointed the Chaldeans to execute ___.
Even with the Chaldeans on the way, Habakkuk says, "We will not die."

cards.text: Then Habakkuk says the LORD's eyes are too pure to look upon evil, and He can't tolerate wrongdoing. You can hear a big SO THEN WHY coming from a mile away.

cards.question: Habakkuk says the LORD's eyes are too pure to look upon evil. So what does Habakkuk ask Him?

answers.text: Why He stays silent while the wicked swallow the righteous
Why He made the horses of the Chaldeans so swift
Why He chose a prophet from such a small town

cards.text: Then Habakkuk paints a picture: the LORD has made men like the fish of the sea, like creeping things with no ruler. Friend, nobody in this picture is enjoying a relaxing fishing trip.

cards.question: If people are like fish in Habakkuk's picture, the foe pulls them all up with a ___.
After hauling people in with his hook and nets, the foe in Habakkuk's picture feels sorry for his catch.
The foe's nets keep bringing in the catch. What does he do with his dragnet?

answers.text: Sacrifices to it and burns incense
Gives it a name and hangs it up
Shares it with the other nations

cards.text: He does it because those nets make his portion sumptuous and his food rich. My oven has baked every batch I ever made, friend, and I've burned incense to it exactly ZERO times.
Habakkuk wraps up with one more question: Will the foe keep emptying his net and slaying nations without mercy? Then, friend, he does something I respect: he stops arguing and starts listening.

cards.question: Habakkuk is ready to listen. Where does he station himself to watch for what the LORD will say?

answers.text: At his guard post on the ramparts
In the temple courts in Jerusalem
In a cave on Mount Horeb

cards.text: Habakkuk up on that wall is every adult who sent a long text and is now staring at the screen, waiting for the three little dots. Then the LORD answers.

cards.question: The LORD tells Habakkuk to keep this vision to himself.
The LORD tells Habakkuk to inscribe the vision clearly on tablets so a ___ may ___ with it.

cards.text: The LORD says the vision awaits an appointed time. It testifies of the end, and it does not lie.

cards.question: The vision awaits an appointed time. What does the LORD tell Habakkuk to do if it seems slow to come?

answers.text: Wait for it because it will surely come
Write it again in bigger letters
Ask another prophet for a new one

cards.text: Then the LORD points to the proud one, whose soul is not upright. And right beside him, He sets someone very different.

cards.question: Next to the proud one, how does the LORD say the righteous will live?

cards.text: Wealth betrays the proud one, and like Death he's never satisfied, gathering all the nations to himself. The LORD isn't done answering Habakkuk yet, friend, so keep your apron on.

findings.problem: The opening card has 4 sentences: the recap of 1:2 and 1:6, the 'from everlasting' line, 'Friend, that's how you open a hard conversation.' and 'Start with who you're talking to.' The limit is 3.

rule.text: **The opening card** can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The opening card states facts from the previous passage, Habakkuk 1:2 and 1:6, and cites them inline. Its verses field says only Habakkuk 1:12. A card's citation is supposed to run from the first verse it uses to the last, but stretching it to 1:2-12 would cite a whole span the card doesn't tell.
findings.question: When a card uses context facts from outside the passage and cites them inline, should its verses field include those verses, or only the passage verses the card tells?

findings.problem: The right answer says the foe sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to it. Habakkuk 1:16 says he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net. The question asks only about the dragnet, so the answer gives the dragnet something the text gives to the fishing net.

rule.text: **Retelling.** Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'sleep' makes 'so a herald may sleep with it,' which reads as silly. It also carries an unfortunate double meaning. It doesn't match the tone of the other answers.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This story card only restates Habakkuk 2:3 and has none of Papa Dorin's voice: no reaction, comparison or storyteller line. It reads as stripped down.

rule.text: **Short, but not stripped down.** A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
